topComments.author: strenholme
topComments.text: With my own MaraDNS, I aggressively optimized the memory usage of blacklist entries by having a single really big malloc() to allocate the memory for the entries, then traversing that memory block for potentially blacklisted entries. When I was using one malloc() per entry, a large blacklist took up 237 megabytes of memory. The same blacklist, once optimized to be loaded with a single malloc() call, only took up 9.5 megabytes of memory. https://samboy.github.io/blog/entries/MaraDNS.html#BlogEntry...

topComments.author: OptionOfT
topComments.text: > we store the records as a single Box<[u8]> containing each record encoded as a 2-byte length prefix followed by its raw bytes. Interestingly this is exactly how netlink works-ish: https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/man3/netlink.3.ht... You start, get the type & length, and then that is how many bytes you read. Some issues with that when you deserialize, from a raw stream in to `[u8; 4096]` buffer, the alignment is only guaranteed to be on 1 byte, not 4 bytes. In practice it is 4 bytes, but if you run those tests with Miri, you'll get yelled at. So the fix there is to declare the buffer with a type that mandates the alignment of the largest type that you're going to be deserializing. So then you start your buffer as follows: `[u32; 1024]`, and with `slice::from_raw_parts` you get to turn that into `[u8; 4096]` with the expected alignment. As an exercise I wrote a streaming parser for netlink, the current existing package serializes everything, all at once.

stories.title: Doctors are finally learning to manage antidepressant withdrawal
stories.author: eutropheon

topComments.author: classichasclass
topComments.text: Though this article concentrates on the SSRIs, other meds like the SNRIs can have a similar or even worse withdrawal effect. We didn't call it "Side Effexor" for nothing. People legitimately need these drugs, including in the short term. The problem for acute stressors once they resolve is how to get them back off.

topComments.author: D-Machine
topComments.text: Best way to manage the withdrawal would be to dramatically reduce them being prescribed in the first place. The linked article says they have "small to moderate effectiveness", but this is being far too generous. The correct way to measure drug effectiveness is if the treatment meets the standard of a minimal important difference. I.e. you measure depression on various rating scales, like the 17-point HAM-D, and research suggests a minimal important difference (i.e. one patients and clinicians can actually notice) needs to be about 3-5 points. But the average effects of almost all antidepressants do not meet these thresholds, i.e. the effect actually appears practically invisible. [1] Then you'll get waffling like "oh, but it really has a big effect for some people", but, well, no, we've looked at that too, and the placebo groups get just as miraculous "big effects", i.e. evidence supporting the idea "they really help some people" is also largely lacking [2-3]. All the other attempted saves ("oh, but eventually you find one that works for you") are also not really well supported either [4]. Like, maybe they really help some people, but it is far, far less clear than most assume, and should be balanced with concerns like withdrawal and serious side effects like emotional blunting and sexual dysfunction. EDIT: And just to be clear to anyone doing a drive-by downvote thinking this is about recent asinine US politics, it emphatically isn't. There are serious methodological concerns here that desperately need to be communicated to the public. [1] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593736/ [2] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7451660/ [3] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33175895/ [4] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11844611/

stories.summary: Medical professionals are increasingly recognizing that withdrawal symptoms from long-term SSRI antidepressant use are more common and severe than previously understood, prompting major health organizations to reconsider prescribing guidelines that have long lacked concrete advice on how to safely discontinue these medications. stories.summary: This article presents a computationally efficient algorithm for calculating the volume of 3D triangulated meshes using the divergence theorem, reducing the problem to a simple loop over triangles with only basic arithmetic operations. The method achieves O(n) performance with approximately 11n floating point operations per n triangles, making it fast enough to process millions of triangles per frame on modest hardware like a Raspberry Pi. stories.summary: OpenAI's Python SDK now uses HTTPX2 instead of HTTPX for HTTP requests, which is installed automatically and requires no changes for users of the default client. However, applications may be affected by HTTPX2's shift from using the certifi CA bundle to the operating-system trust store, requiring explicit certificate configuration in minimal containers or corporate proxy environments. Users providing custom HTTP clients should migrate to HTTPX2 configuration objects using the provided helper classes.

stories.summary: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are emerging as a promising alternative to conventional nuclear plants, offering cheaper and faster construction through factory-built, modular components that can be assembled on-site. Companies like Kairos Power are developing SMRs using innovative fuels (like TRISO pebbles) and coolants (such as molten salt) that enhance safety and efficiency, with significant government funding driving deployment despite some critics' concerns about long-term cost-effectiveness. stories.title: Show HN: Talos – An AI agent with a permission kernel between model and shell
stories.author: kurdman_007

topComments.author: kurdman_007
topComments.text: Hi HN — maker here. I built Talos because I wanted to hand an agent a terminal without handing it my trust model. Every tool call (read, write, exec, delegate) passes a small deterministic kernel, ~645 lines of Python, that returns allow, needs-human or deny. Unattended runs can't ask, so needs-human becomes deny. The agent can never grant itself anything. Around that kernel: 23 gated tools, a UID-separated worker for delegated code, MCP servers confined to that worker from an operator-owned registry (no marketplace, no third-party code in the agent process), a hash-chained audit log, Ed25519-signed updates verified before anything unpacks, and a read-only live dashboard that has no approve button, by design. Numbers the CI enforces on every page of the site: 2063 tests, 179/179 adversarial cases, 645 kernel lines, 0 inbound ports. The site has a browser reimplementation of the policy kernel you can poke at without installing anything, a replayed real session, and an honest comparison to OpenClaw and Hermes — including what Talos doesn't have (breadth; that's doctrine, not backlog). Happy to answer anything — especially the parts where the design is wrong. Site: https://talos-agent.ch — Source (MIT): https://github.com/talos-kernel/talos

stories.summary: Talos is an AI agent that implements a "permission kernel" between Claude and shell access, requiring every tool call to pass through deterministic security checks that authorize individual effects with specific arguments, time limits, and sandboxing. The system is designed with security-first architecture, distinguishing between read operations (allowed freely), reversible write operations (require approval), and dangerous exec operations (sandboxed or refused), with transparency features like adversarial testing and a public ledger of security decisions. It's installable and supports multiple channels (terminal, Telegram, email, WhatsApp) while preventing unauthorized file access, credential exposure, and system damage through path restrictions and mandatory human approval for irreversible actions.

stories.summary: Bhartrhari's Paradox, identified by a fifth-century Indian philosopher, describes a logical contradiction: some things are unnameable, yet proving this requires naming those very things. Any argument attempting to demonstrate unnameability paradoxically involves repeatedly referencing the supposedly unnameable things it seeks to establish.

stories.title: Terry Rozier and the Teleprompt Operator
stories.author: surprisetalk
stories.summary:
# Summary

NBA player Terry Rozier was indicted in 2025 for tipping off a friend about leaving a game early so he could place $200,000+ in insider bets, exploiting the massive growth of legal sports gambling. The article argues that while legalization makes it easier to detect fraud, it simultaneously enables larger-scale insider betting schemes by providing the liquidity needed to accommodate six-figure wagers—a problem that extends beyond sports to prediction markets, where a White House teleprompter operator recently bet on presidential speech content. The piece suggests that sports gambling legalization creates a dangerous paradox: better monitoring of fraud but also easier execution of it at unprecedented scales.
